title: List Comprehension
body:
Notation for building a list by describing it rather than by looping to fill one. It is
set-builder notation from [[Sets]] with the braces changed to brackets:

$$\{\, x^2 \mid x \in \mathbb{N},\ x \text{ even} \,\}$$

```haskell
[x ^ 2 | x <- [1 ..], even x]
```

Read it left to right as three parts: the **output expression** (`x ^ 2`), one or more
**generators** (`x <- [1..]`, "draw x from"), and any number of **guards** (`even x`, a
boolean filter).

```haskell
[ (a, b, c) | c <- [1 .. 20]
            , b <- [1 .. c]
            , a <- [1 .. b]
            , a*a + b*b == c*c ]      -- Pythagorean triples up to 20
```

Multiple generators nest, leftmost outermost, so the last one varies fastest. That is exactly a
nested loop, written without saying `for` and without an index variable to get wrong.

## It is `map` and `filter`

Every comprehension desugars into the two list functions, and it is worth being able to do the
translation both ways:

| Comprehension | Equivalent |
|---|---|
| `[f x \| x <- xs]` | `map f xs` |
| `[x \| x <- xs, p x]` | `filter p xs` |
| `[f x \| x <- xs, p x]` | `map f (filter p xs)` |
| `[(x, y) \| x <- xs, y <- ys]` | `concatMap (\x -> map (\y -> (x, y)) ys) xs` |

That last row is the one worth staring at. Two generators become `concatMap`, which is
**exactly `>>=` for lists**, so a list comprehension is `do`-notation for the list [[Monad]]
in disguise. The generator arrow `<-` is the same arrow, and it is the same "take every
possible value, keep going" idea that [[Nondeterminism]] describes for an [[NFA]]. Neither the
comprehension nor the monad is the fundamental one; they are two syntaxes over `concatMap`.

## Laziness makes the infinite case work

`[1 ..]` is an infinite list, and the comprehension above is still a usable value because
nothing is computed until demanded:

```haskell
take 5 [x ^ 2 | x <- [1 ..], even x]    -- [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]
```

The generator produces elements on demand and stops when the consumer stops asking. See
[[Lazy Evaluation]]. This is the payoff that separates a comprehension from a loop: you can
describe the whole infinite set and let the consumer decide how much of it exists.

A guard that is never satisfied will hang forever on an infinite generator, which is the price
of the same property. `[x | x <- [1..], x < 0]` does not return an empty list, it never returns.

## Elsewhere

Python borrowed the syntax almost unchanged (`[x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]`), which
is why it feels familiar before you have written any Haskell. [[SQL]] is the same idea with the
clauses reordered: `SELECT` is the output expression, `FROM` is the generator, `WHERE` is the
guard, and the [[Regular Expressions|declarative]] point is identical, describe the result and
let something else pick the loop.

## Core Facts to Know

- Three parts: output expression, generators (`x <- xs`), guards (boolean filters).
- It is set-builder notation from [[Sets]] with brackets instead of braces.
- Multiple generators nest, leftmost outermost; the rightmost varies fastest.
- One generator plus a guard is `map` and `filter`; two generators is `concatMap`.
- `concatMap` is `>>=` for lists, so a comprehension is the list [[Monad]] in other syntax.
- With [[Lazy Evaluation]] the generator may be infinite, as long as the consumer is finite.
- An unsatisfiable guard over an infinite generator does not return empty, it does not return.
- [[SQL]]'s `SELECT` / `FROM` / `WHERE` is the same three parts in a different order.
